questions.q: Which conditions are used for standard enthalpy changes?
questions.solution: Standard conditions are a pressure of \(100\ \text{kPa}\) and a stated temperature, usually \(298\ \text{K}\), with every substance in its standard state. (\(273\ \text{K}\) and \(101\ \text{kPa}\) are the old conditions for gas volumes, not for enthalpy changes.)

questions.q: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of ethanol?
questions.solution: Enthalpy of formation is for one mole of the compound formed from its elements in their standard states: carbon as solid graphite, hydrogen and oxygen as diatomic gases. So \(\mathrm{2C(s) + 3H_{2}(g) + \frac{1}{2}O_{2}(g) \rightarrow C_{2}H_{5}OH(l)}\). (Doubling to avoid the half makes two moles of ethanol.)

questions.q: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy change of combustion of propane?
questions.solution: Combustion is complete burning of one mole of the substance in oxygen under standard conditions. At \(298\ \text{K}\) water is a liquid, so it must be \(\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}\), and the carbon must end up as \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\). So \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}(g) + 5O_{2}(g) \rightarrow 3CO_{2}(g) + 4H_{2}O(l)}\). (Writing water as a gas is the most common slip.)

questions.q: Which is the definition of the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation?

options.A: The enthalpy change when one mole of acid reacts completely with alkali under standard conditions
options.B: The enthalpy change when one mole of salt is formed from an acid and an alkali under standard conditions
options.C: The energy released when one mole of hydrogen ions is removed from an acid
options.D: The enthalpy change when an acid and an alkali react to form one mole of water under standard conditions

questions.solution: Neutralisation is defined per mole of water formed, \(\mathrm{H^{+}(aq) + OH^{-}(aq) \rightarrow H_{2}O(l)}\), under standard conditions. Defining it per mole of acid would give twice the value for sulfuric acid, which releases two moles of water per mole. (Per mole of salt fails for the same reason.)

questions.q: \(50.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(1.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) hydrochloric acid is mixed with \(50.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(1.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) sodium hydroxide. The temperature rises by \(6.8\ \text{K}\). What is the enthalpy change per mole of water formed? (Assume the solution has density \(1.00\ \text{g cm}^{-3}\) and \(c = 4.18\ \text{J g}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}\).)
questions.solution: The mass heated is the whole mixture, 100 g: \(q = mc\Delta T = 100 \times 4.18 \times 6.8 = 2842\ \text{J}\). Water formed = \(1.00 \times 0.0500 = 0.0500\ \text{mol}\). The temperature rose, so the reaction is exothermic: \(\Delta H = -\frac{2.842}{0.0500}\) = \(-56.8\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). (Using only 50 g of solution leads to \(-28.4\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).)

questions.q: Burning 0.460 g of ethanol (\(M_{\text{r}} = 46.0\)) heats 150 g of water by \(12.5\ \text{K}\). What value does this give for the enthalpy change of combustion of ethanol? (\(c = 4.18\ \text{J g}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}\))
questions.solution: Heat absorbed by the water: \(q = 150 \times 4.18 \times 12.5 = 7838\ \text{J}\). Amount of ethanol: \(\frac{0.460}{46.0} = 0.0100\ \text{mol}\). Combustion is exothermic: \(\Delta H = -\frac{7.838}{0.0100}\) = \(-784\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). (Using the mass of ethanol, not the water, in \(q = mc\Delta T\) is a common slip; leaving out the division by the amount leads to \(-7.84\).)

questions.q: A student's value for the enthalpy change of combustion of ethanol by calorimetry is much less exothermic than the data-book value, \(-1367\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Which pair of reasons explains this?

options.A: The thermometer was read before the highest temperature was reached, and the mass of ethanol burned was measured too low.
options.B: Heat was lost to the surroundings rather than to the water, and the combustion was incomplete.
options.C: The water was stirred, and the flame was too close to the beaker.
options.D: Water formed in the reaction was a liquid, and the room was warmer than 298 K.

questions.solution: Heat that escapes to the air and the apparatus never reaches the water, so \(\Delta T\) is too small. Incomplete combustion (soot, CO) releases less energy than complete combustion. Both make the value less exothermic. Measuring too little ethanol would make the value more exothermic, not less. (Stirring improves accuracy rather than causing the error.)

questions.q: Use the enthalpies of formation to find \(\Delta H\) for \(\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}(s) + 3CO(g) \rightarrow 2Fe(s) + 3CO_{2}(g)}\). (\(\Delta_{\text{f}}H\) in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): \(\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}(s)}\) −824, \(\mathrm{CO(g)}\) −111, \(\mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}\) −394)
questions.solution: \(\Delta H = \sum \Delta_{\text{f}}H(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta_{\text{f}}H(\text{reactants})\). Products: \(3 \times (-394) = -1182\) (iron is an element, so 0). Reactants: \(-824 + 3 \times (-111) = -1157\). So \(\Delta H = -1182 - (-1157)\) = \(-25\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). (Subtracting the other way round leads to +25; forgetting the 3s leads to +541.)

questions.q: Use the enthalpies of combustion to find the enthalpy change of formation of ethanol, \(\mathrm{2C(s) + 3H_{2}(g) + \frac{1}{2}O_{2}(g) \rightarrow C_{2}H_{5}OH(l)}\). (\(\Delta_{\text{c}}H\) in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): C(s) −394, \(\mathrm{H_{2}(g)}\) −286, \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}OH(l)}\) −1367)
questions.solution: With combustion data, \(\Delta H = \sum \Delta_{\text{c}}H(\text{reactants}) - \sum \Delta_{\text{c}}H(\text{products})\). Reactants: \(2(-394) + 3(-286) = -1646\). Product: −1367. So \(\Delta_{\text{f}}H = -1646 - (-1367)\) = \(-279\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). (Using products minus reactants, as for formation data, leads to +279.)

questions.q: Which is a statement of Hess's law?

options.A: The enthalpy change of a reaction depends on the route taken, provided the temperature is constant.
options.B: Energy is released when bonds form and absorbed when bonds break.
options.C: The enthalpy change of a reaction equals the sum of the enthalpies of formation of the products.
options.D: The enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken, provided the initial and final conditions are the same.

questions.solution: Hess's law: the enthalpy change for a reaction is the same whichever route is taken from reactants to products, as long as the start and end conditions are the same. It follows from conservation of energy, and is what lets enthalpy cycles find changes that cannot be measured directly. (The sum of the products' enthalpies of formation is only part of a Hess calculation.)

questions.q: Use the bond enthalpies to find \(\Delta H\) for \(\mathrm{H_{2}(g) + Cl_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2HCl(g)}\). (Bond enthalpies in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 432)
questions.solution: Bonds broken: \(436 + 243 = 679\ \text{kJ}\). Bonds formed: \(2 \times 432 = 864\ \text{kJ}\). \(\Delta H\) = broken − formed = \(679 - 864\) = \(-185\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). (Forming only one H–Cl bond leads to +247.)

questions.q: Use the mean bond enthalpies to estimate \(\Delta H\) for \(\mathrm{CH_{4}(g) + 2O_{2}(g) \rightarrow CO_{2}(g) + 2H_{2}O(g)}\). (In \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O–H 464)
questions.solution: Broken: \(4 \times 413 + 2 \times 498 = 2648\ \text{kJ}\). Formed: \(2 \times 805 + 4 \times 464 = 3466\ \text{kJ}\) (two C=O, and two O–H in each of two water molecules). \(\Delta H = 2648 - 3466\) = \(-818\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). (Counting one O–H per water molecule leads to +110.)

questions.q: For \(\mathrm{N_{2}H_{4}(g) + O_{2}(g) \rightarrow N_{2}(g) + 2H_{2}O(g)}\), \(\Delta H = -583\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Use the data to find the mean bond enthalpy of the N–H bond. (In \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): N–N 158, O=O 498, N≡N 945, O–H 464)
questions.solution: Hydrazine, \(\mathrm{H_{2}N{-}NH_{2}}\), has four N–H bonds and one N–N bond. Broken: \(4x + 158 + 498\). Formed: \(945 + 4 \times 464 = 2801\). So \(4x + 656 - 2801 = -583\), giving \(4x = 1562\) and \(x\) = 390.5, about \(391\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). (Taking \(\Delta H\) as +583 leads to 682; forgetting to divide by 4 leads to 1562.)

questions.q: The enthalpy change of combustion of methane calculated from mean bond enthalpies differs from the value found from enthalpies of formation. Which statement best explains why?

options.A: Bond enthalpies are measured at constant volume, but enthalpies of formation at constant pressure.
options.B: Enthalpies of formation are less accurate because they are found by experiment.
options.C: Mean bond enthalpies are averages over many different compounds, so they are not exact for the bonds in these particular molecules.
options.D: Methane contains only single bonds, so its bonds cannot be broken completely.

questions.solution: A C–H bond's enthalpy varies slightly from one molecule to another, so data books give a mean over many compounds. Using means gives only an estimate for any particular reaction. The method also assumes every substance is a gas. (Enthalpies of formation are specific to each compound, so they give the more accurate value.)

questions.q: Which statement is correct for an endothermic reaction?

options.A: The products have less enthalpy than the reactants, and the temperature of the surroundings rises.
options.B: The products have more enthalpy than the reactants, and the temperature of the surroundings rises.
options.C: The products have less enthalpy than the reactants, and \(\Delta H\) is positive.
options.D: The products have more enthalpy than the reactants, \(\Delta H\) is positive, and the temperature of the surroundings falls.

questions.solution: An endothermic reaction takes in heat energy from its surroundings, so the surroundings cool. On an enthalpy level diagram the products sit above the reactants, and \(\Delta H = H_{\text{products}} - H_{\text{reactants}}\) is positive. (A rise in the temperature of the surroundings means the reaction is exothermic.)

questions.q: An enthalpy change, \(\Delta H\), is the heat energy change measured under which condition?
questions.solution: Enthalpy change is defined as the heat energy change at constant pressure. Standard enthalpy changes add a set pressure of 100 kPa and a stated temperature. (The heat change at constant volume is a different quantity, the internal energy change.)

questions.q: Excess zinc powder is added to \(50.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.200\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) copper(II) sulfate solution, and the temperature rises by \(10.2\ \text{K}\). What is the enthalpy change for \(\mathrm{Zn(s) + CuSO_{4}(aq) \rightarrow ZnSO_{4}(aq) + Cu(s)}\)? (\(c = 4.18\ \text{J g}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}\); density of solution \(1.00\ \text{g cm}^{-3}\))
questions.solution: \(q = 50.0 \times 4.18 \times 10.2 = 2132\ \text{J}\). Zinc is in excess, so the copper(II) sulfate limits the reaction: \(0.200 \times 0.0500 = 0.0100\ \text{mol}\). \(\Delta H = -\frac{2.132}{0.0100}\) = \(-213\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). (Stopping at the heat released, in kJ, leads to −2.13.)

questions.q: The enthalpy change of solution of anhydrous copper(II) sulfate, \(\mathrm{CuSO_{4}(s)}\), is \(-66.5\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), and that of the hydrated salt, \(\mathrm{CuSO_{4} \cdot 5H_{2}O(s)}\), is \(+11.7\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). What is \(\Delta H\) for \(\mathrm{CuSO_{4}(s) + 5H_{2}O(l) \rightarrow CuSO_{4} \cdot 5H_{2}O(s)}\)?
questions.solution: Both salts dissolve to give the same solution. Route 1: anhydrous to solution, −66.5. Route 2: anhydrous to hydrated (\(\Delta H\)), then hydrated to solution, +11.7. By Hess's law \(\Delta H + 11.7 = -66.5\), so \(\Delta H\) = \(-78.2\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). (Adding the two values leads to −54.8.)
